title: Former PR firm director's wrongful dismissal claim fails after she covertly recorded meeting; All 10 Singapore-based firms respond to NEA haze law notices, most saying they will cooperate: Singapore live news

A tribunal magistrate has dismissed a former PR firm director's wrongful dismissal claim over a covertly recorded company meeting. (PHOTO: ROSLAN RAHMAN/AFP via Getty Images) A magistrate has ruled that secretly recording a company meeting could amount to misconduct that justifies immediate dismissal. The ruling threw out a wrongful dismissal claim by a former managing director of a public relations firm, identified only as JJT in court documents. In a judgment dated 23 Oct, Tribunal Magistrate Kerry Chan noted that no reported Singapore judgments had addressed the issue. The Employment Act allows employers to dismiss staff without notice for misconduct, she said, so the question was whether the recording warranted immediate dismissal.
 The Straits Times reported that JJT was told on 23 Feb that her employment was being terminated without cause. She could serve a three-month notice period or go on immediate garden leave with two months' salary, and chose to work until 22 May. Days later, she received a formal misconduct warning over several lapses during her notice period. The firm's leadership cited unauthorised contact with a client, reaching out to a colleague on his day off, and attending a business meeting where she forgot her own team member's name.
 All 10 Singapore-based companies issued notices under the haze law have acknowledged the National Environment Agency's (NEA) requests for information on their links to fires in Indonesia. Most have said they will cooperate.

First Resources followed at 1.15am on 24 Oct, agreeing to provide the necessary details. Bumitama Agri and its subsidiaries said in a filing that afternoon that they would provide the requested documents and information.
 Asia Pulp & Paper told The Straits Times at about 6.30pm that day that it was cooperating with the authorities, and Golden Agri International later said the same. Kencana Agri, owned by the Maknawi family, said in a filing on 25 Oct that it would cooperate fully.
 Three firms did not explicitly say they would cooperate.

 Live coverage is over 10 updates Featured Tue, Oct 27, 2026 02:15 AM UTC Former PR firm director’s wrongful dismissal claim fails after she covertly recorded meeting
 A tribunal magistrate has dismissed a former PR firm director's wrongful dismissal claim over a covertly recorded company meeting. (PHOTO: Roslan RAHMAN / AFP via Getty Images)
 A magistrate has ruled that secretly recording a company meeting could amount to misconduct that justifies immediate dismissal. The ruling threw out a wrongful dismissal claim by a former managing director of a public relations firm, identified only as JJT in court documents. In a judgment dated 23 Oct, Tribunal Magistrate Kerry Chan noted that no reported Singapore judgments had addressed the issue. The Employment Act allows employers to dismiss staff without notice for misconduct, she said, so the question was whether the recording warranted immediate dismissal.
 The Straits Times reported that JJT was told on 23 Feb that her employment was being terminated without cause. She could serve a three-month notice period or go on immediate garden leave with two months' salary, and chose to work until 22 May. Days later, she received a formal misconduct warning over several lapses during her notice period. The firm's leadership cited unauthorised contact with a client, reaching out to a colleague on his day off, and attending a business meeting where she forgot her own team member's name.
 On 3 March, JJT attended a regular weekly meeting with the firm's president and chief human resources officer, where she responded to the allegations. She recorded the conversation on her phone. The president noticed the recording on the screen as she showed a WhatsApp message she had sent to her colleague about her termination. She then deleted the recording and left her phone outside the room. The president later asked her to pause work and explain in writing what had happened, including whether she had recorded internal discussions before.
 On 6 March, she was handed an immediate termination letter saying the unauthorised recording was misconduct and a fundamental breach of trust and confidence.
 JJT argued that the dismissal was wrongful, saying she had placed her phone on the table to record openly, solely to help prepare an accurate written response. She said she deleted the recording as soon as she was asked, and that no confidential client information, financial figures, or other business information had been discussed. She also contended that the firm used the incident to deprive her of the salary she would have earned until 22 May.
 The firm, which was not named in court documents, said JJT was not an ordinary rank-and-file employee. It argued that if a senior leader covertly recorded her own management, every conversation afterwards would come into doubt. It added that as the most senior member of her business unit, she was held to the highest standard of professional judgment, and her contract named a breach of its confidentiality provisions as cause for termination without notice. Chan accepted that the firm understandably had stringent confidentiality standards, as its public relations work involved being entrusted with clients' confidential information.
 The meeting was convened to discuss the firm's business, so it was irrelevant that only JJT's lapses had been discussed when the recording was noticed, Chan said. With the recording deleted, she could not determine its true purpose, and questioned why one was needed when JJT was already reading from prepared notes.
 Some acts can destroy trust in an employment relationship whatever the employee's intentions, she said, and the covert recording was "sufficient to destroy the trust and confidence in this employment relationship". She stressed that this does not mean every covert recording warrants dismissal, as each case turns on its own facts.

 Featured Tue, Oct 27, 2026 08:30 AM UTC Apple to replace iPhone Duo handsets with screen faults days after launch
 Photos shared online show lines on the inner display of Apple's iPhone Duo, days after the foldable went on sale. (PHOTO: Chris Jung/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
 Apple will replace iPhone Duo handsets that have developed screen problems , just days after the highly anticipated smartphone went on sale. The company said it is aware of "an issue impacting the inner display on a small number" of the phones, and urged affected users to contact it for a replacement.
 The BBC reported that photos posted on social media show lines across the screens of Apple's first foldable device. The phone starts at £1,999 (about S$3,450) in the UK.
 Some owners also shared images of cracks along the crease at the centre of the screen, while others described a crunching noise when opening the phone. One user, Justin Lokos, posted an image of a handset with lines across the right side of its display. He later shared a photo of a replacement next to the faulty unit and thanked an Apple store in New York for its help.
 The extent of the problem remains unclear. Apple did not say how many devices were affected, and some images of faulty phones may have been created using artificial intelligence.
 The Duo is Apple's first major iPhone redesign in almost two decades. It was unveiled by new chief executive John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September. Its 7.6-inch inner display is held together by a central hinge, a complex piece of engineering that has led to similar flaws in some rivals' foldables. Samsung's first foldable, the Galaxy Fold, suffered an early setback in 2019 when reviewers reported broken screens.

 Tue, Oct 27, 2026 09:37 AM UTC Singapore solar push: Plans for home owners, public buildings and heritage roofs
 An AI-generated image of solar panels hanging between industrial buildings at 15 Woodlands Loop. (PHOTO: The Straits Times)
 Singapore is stepping up its solar push , with plans that include hanging panels between buildings and trialling clay-like solar tiles for heritage buildings. Minister of State for Energy, Trade and Industry Gan Siow Huang announced the plans on 27 Oct at the Singapore International Energy Week.
 The authorities are working with government agencies, companies, and home owners to meet the renewed target of 4 gigawatt-peak (GWp) of solar energy by 2035. That is about 5 per cent of Singapore's projected electricity demand for that year. The country now generates about 2.3GWp and aims to reach 3GWp by the end of 2030.
 The Energy Market Authority (EMA) will partner the Sustainable Energy Association of Singapore to develop a digital portal for private home owners. It will provide solar-related information and services, help home owners connect with installers, and explore group purchase opportunities. There are more than 8,000 residential solar installations now.
 EMA will also work with the Energy Research Institute @ NTU to map the capacity of local electricity networks. The study will look at how landed housing estates can take more solar installations and cope with more power flowing back to the grid.
 On 27 Oct, EMA also launched an initiative to pool demand for solar across public and government buildings. A panel of solar installers will be appointed to help agencies assess the solar potential of their premises and develop tailored solutions. Agencies can also explore options such as solar roofs at car parks and replacing windows or building facades with special solar panels.
 JTC Corporation, which is responsible for 45 per cent of Singapore's current solar capacity, is piloting ways to harness solar energy from unconventional spaces in its industrial estates. In one project, panels will be suspended between two existing industrial buildings at 15 Woodlands Loop. Renewable energy company EDP APAC will build and test the structure over 15 months from October.
 JTC said such structures face engineering and operational challenges. They must carry their own weight and that of the panels while withstanding wind forces at height.
 JTC also announced an innovation call on 27 Oct for portable solar solutions at construction sites with limited access to the national grid. One option is deploying panels from containers fitted with mobile energy storage systems. Gan said this would help temporary worksites that currently rely heavily on diesel generators.
 EMA is also partnering the Singapore Land Authority and CSEM, a Swiss technology innovation centre, to pilot solar photovoltaic (PV) roof tiles on heritage buildings. The tiles are designed to resemble traditional clay roof tiles, so a larger roof area can generate clean electricity while older buildings keep their character, EMA said.
 Gan said Singapore is "pushing all boundaries and surfaces, literally" to harness solar. She noted that there are limits, however, because of land scarcity and intermittency from cloud cover. At most, she said, solar can meet 10 per cent of Singapore's electricity needs by 2050, the year the country has pledged to reach net zero carbon emissions.

 Tue, Oct 27, 2026 05:48 AM UTC Jay-Z to take Super Bowl half-time stage himself after years of helping pick its performers
 Jay-Z will take the Super Bowl half-time stage in February 2027, having helped pick the show's performers for years through his company Roc Nation. (Photo by Steph Chambers - FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images)
 Rapper Jay-Z will perform at the Super Bowl half-time show in February, the NFL announced. He has been involved in the show for years but has never performed at the NFL championship game before. His company, Roc Nation, has produced the half-time show since 2019, and he plays a key role in choosing each year's performer. In a statement, the NFL said speculation over who Jay-Z might bring on as guest stars would now begin, adding that his wife, Beyoncé, would of course top that list.
 The announcement came after Jay-Z performed two shows last weekend at the Los Angeles stadium where the Super Bowl will be played. The shows were part of a tour celebrating the 30th anniversary of his debut album Reasonable Doubt. He said the road from Reasonable Doubt to the half-time stage spans 30 years of music, work, and culture, and called the run a "dream come true".
 NFL commissioner Roger Goodell said his only request when the league first agreed with Roc Nation to produce the show was that Jay-Z take the stage himself one day, whenever the moment felt right to him. He added that he could not be more excited for fans around the world to experience the artistry, creativity, and cultural impact Jay-Z will bring.
 Jay-Z follows recent half-time performers including Bad Bunny, Kendrick Lamar, Usher, Rihanna, and The Weeknd. Lamar's 2025 show was the most watched half-time show in history and won an Emmy for outstanding music direction. Jay-Z was the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame, and his accolades include 25 Grammy awards and induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.

 Tue, Oct 27, 2026 05:32 AM UTC Trump says he doesn’t want Norwegian immigrants because he didn’t win Nobel Peace Prize
 US President Donald Trump took aim at Norway over the Nobel Peace Prize during a rally on Sunday, weeks ahead of the US midterm elections. (PHOTO: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
 US President Donald Trump has attacked Norway at a campaign rally, calling it a "s***house country" and saying he does not want Norwegian immigrants because he was not awarded the Nobel Peace Prize . Speaking on Sunday in Port Huron, Michigan, ahead of the US midterm elections on 3 Nov, he said he would welcome immigrants from certain countries, but not Norway.
 There was no official indication of a new US policy on Norwegian immigrants. Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide responded on Monday, telling national broadcaster NRK that the Nobel Committee is independent. He said Trump knows this, and that Norway has reminded him of it.
 Trump has made no secret of his wish to win the prize since returning to the White House in January 2025. This year's recipient was South African judge and former UN rights chief Navi Pillay . Trump has described the committee's choice as disgraceful and embarrassing, and argued that the award should have gone to him.
 He also came under fire in 2018, during his first term, for using similar vulgar expressions to refer to Haiti and certain African countries.

 Tue, Oct 27, 2026 03:34 AM UTC 60,000 Microsoft employees offered voluntary exit packages as it pours money into AI
 Microsoft's voluntary exit offer is open to staff on select teams in four countries, at vice president level and below. (PHOTO: Getty Images)
 Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, or around 27 per cent of its workforce, as it looks to cut costs while pouring money into artificial intelligence (AI) . The company announced the offer on Monday (26 Oct).
 Staff on select teams in the United States, Canada, India, and Britain at vice president level and below are eligible, a Microsoft spokesperson said. Some groups are excluded, including some working on data centres, sales, and marketing. In a memo to employees, chief people officer Amy Coleman said the offer is part of how the company is evolving its approach to change. She said it creates more flexibility and, where possible, more ways for staff to "shape their next chapter".
 This is Microsoft's second voluntary buyout offer this year. In April, it reportedly offered about seven per cent of its US workforce the option to retire early. CNBC reported that around 30 per cent of those eligible took the plan.
 Regulatory filings show Microsoft had 223,000 employees globally at the end of June, down from 228,000 at the end of 2025. The company is expected to report quarterly earnings later this week.

 Tue, Oct 27, 2026 03:30 AM UTC Alex Eala overwhelms British teenager in 75 minutes in Tokyo, sets up Talia Gibson clash
 Alex Eala, the eighth seed at the Pan Pacific Open, beat British teenager Mika Stojsavljevic in straight sets to reach the second round in Tokyo. (PHOTO: Taylor Hill/Getty Images)
 Alex Eala opened her Pan Pacific Open campaign in Tokyo with a commanding 6-1, 6-2 win over British teenager Mika Stojsavljevic on Monday. The eighth seed from the Philippines advanced to the second round of the WTA 500 tournament in 75 minutes. Her next opponent is Australian Talia Gibson.
 Heavy reported that Eala raced to a 5-0 lead in the opening set and put pressure on Stojsavljevic's serve. The 17-year-old wild card, who won the 2024 US Open girls' singles title, hit 24 winners to Eala's eight but committed 41 unforced errors to Eala's 11. Eala, 21, converted four of seven break points and saved all three she faced.
 In her on-court interview, Eala said it was important to be focused on every single point. She praised her opponent's level and said she was sure the two would meet "many, many more times".
 Gibson, ranked No. 38, beat compatriot Daria Kasatkina 6-0, 7-5 on Monday to reach the round of 16. Eala has beaten her twice before, in 2023, at ITF tournaments in Palma del Río, Spain, and Aldershot, England. She won one meeting 6-3, 6-1 and the other 4-6, 6-4, 6-3.
 A win over Gibson would send Eala into the quarterfinals, where she could face Diana Shnaider. Shnaider eliminated her from the Ningbo Open earlier this month. Monday's result came after early exits in Wuhan and Ningbo, in what Heavy described as an uneven stretch of performances in Asia.

 Tue, Oct 27, 2026 02:31 AM UTC From 1 Nov, travellers in Japan must pay tax upfront and claim refunds at the airport
 Japan's revised tax-free shopping rules, which take effect on 1 Nov, bring new steps for tourists at both stores and airports. (PHOTO: Getty Images)
 From 1 Nov, travellers shopping in Japan will have to pay full price in-store and claim their tax refund at the airport before leaving. Eligible purchases are currently exempt from the 10 per cent consumption tax at the point of sale. The change is aimed at curbing abuse by travellers who buy goods tax-free, then illegally resell them for a profit equal to the tax.
 The Straits Times likened the new process to Singapore's goods and services tax refund system for tourists. According to Japan's National Tax Agency and the Japan Tax-free Shop websites, purchases totalling 5,000 yen (S$40) or more per store per day are eligible. Gold and platinum bullion and airport duty-free items are excluded. Travellers must present their passport at eligible shops so the purchase can be registered.
 Under the pay-first, refund-later system, travellers must go through customs inspection at the airport within 90 days of purchase. They will have to show their passport at a tax-free procedure terminal. All items listed on a receipt must be presented for inspection. If even one is missing, perhaps because it has been consumed, none of the goods on that receipt will qualify for a refund.
 The terminals are at the international departure lobby. Travellers can also complete the process online through Visit Japan Web at Narita, Haneda, Kansai, Chubu, Fukuoka, New Chitose, and Naha airports. However, they must be within the departure lobby areas with dedicated Wi-Fi, up to the security checkpoint. Luggage should not be checked in before the inspection, as goods may need to be examined and checked baggage cannot be retrieved. Travellers should arrive early to allow enough time.
 The quantity of goods bought tax-free is limited to what a traveller can personally take out of Japan. This means goods shipped separately to Singapore will not qualify for a refund. The new system removes the daily purchase limit of 500,000 yen on consumables such as alcohol and cosmetics, and special packaging is no longer required.
 Travellers who have consumed all or part of these items should not complete the tax-free procedure and should instead report them to a customs officer at the counter. Items left behind in Japan after passing inspection will incur consumption tax equal to the exempted amount, along with penalties.

 Tue, Oct 27, 2026 02:23 AM UTC Singapore air quality stays healthy overnight, with normal PM2.5 and good-to-moderate PSI
 Air quality across Singapore stayed healthy overnight, with PM2.5 readings in the normal range and the 24-hour PSI in the good-to-moderate band. (PHOTO: Then Chih Wey/Xinhua via Getty Images)
 Singapore's air quality remained healthy overnight, with hourly PM2.5 readings in the normal range and the 24-hour PSI in the good-to-moderate band across the island. At 6am on 27 Oct, the one-hour PM2.5 readings in all five regions ranged between 14 and 32. The 24-hour PSI stood between 62 and 72.
 PM2.5 readings are gauged hourly and reflect current air quality. Scores from zero to 55 are normal, while those between 56 and 150 indicate an elevated concentration of fine particles. The PSI is a 24-hour rolling average of six key air pollutants. Air quality is considered good to moderate when it is between zero and 100, and unhealthy between 101 and 200. Once it breaches the unhealthy threshold, people, especially the elderly, children, and those with health issues, should start scaling down outdoor activities.
 Residents saw some respite over the weekend after weeks of bad air quality . PM2.5 levels stood in the normal range for most parts of the country, although the 24-hour PSI readings remained unhealthy in some areas.
 In its daily haze advisory on the evening of 26 Oct, the National Environment Agency (NEA) forecast the PSI for 27 Oct to be in the good-to-moderate range of 60 to 90. Smoke haze was observed but confined over Kalimantan on 26 Oct, while it was cloudy over Singapore. The NEA said the likelihood of smoke haze affecting Singapore on 27 Oct is low, with winds expected from the north-east or south-east and showers expected over and near the island.
 Winds are forecast to become variable on 28 and 29 Oct, with showers expected over Singapore and the surrounding region. The wet conditions should help keep hotspot and smoke haze activity suppressed, the NEA said.

 Tue, Oct 27, 2026 02:16 AM UTC All 10 Singapore-based firms respond to NEA haze law notices, most saying they will cooperate
 The National Environment Agency has asked 10 Singapore-based firms for information on their links to fires in Indonesia under the haze law. (PHOTO: Then Chih Wey/Xinhua via Getty Images)
 All 10 Singapore-based companies issued notices under the haze law have acknowledged the National Environment Agency's (NEA) requests for information on their links to fires in Indonesia. Most have said they will cooperate.
 Wilmar International was the first to announce it would comply, in a filing close to midnight on 23 Oct, about three hours after the NEA sent the notices. First Resources followed at 1.15am on 24 Oct, agreeing to provide the necessary details. Bumitama Agri and its subsidiaries said in a filing that afternoon that they would provide the requested documents and information.
 Asia Pulp & Paper told The Straits Times at about 6.30pm that day that it was cooperating with the authorities, and Golden Agri International later said the same. Kencana Agri, owned by the Maknawi family, said in a filing on 25 Oct that it would cooperate fully.
 Three firms did not explicitly say they would cooperate: Indofood Agri Resources, TSH Global Plantation, and TSH Oversea. Indofood Agri Resources said in a filing on 25 Oct that it received the notice on 23 Oct and would give more details when there were material updates. The two TSH firms were the last to respond, on 26 Oct, through Malaysian firm TSH Resources, which oversees them. In a Singapore Exchange filing at 8.12am, TSH Resources said the subsidiaries were notified to provide documents and information under Section 10 of the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act (THPA) by 2 Nov. It said it is reviewing the notice and will engage with the agency accordingly.
 Under Section 10, representatives of non-compliant firms can face a fine of up to $5,000, a jail term of up to one month, or both. Separately, entities found guilty of causing or contributing to the haze can be fined up to $100,000 for every day the pollution persists, capped at $2 million.
 The NEA issued the notices on the night of 23 Oct to Asia Pulp & Paper Company, Asia Pulp & Paper Company (China), Bumitama Agri, Golden Agri International, First Resources, Indofood Agri Resources, Kencana Agri, TSH Global Plantation, TSH Oversea, and Wilmar International. All 10 are in the oil palm or forestry business and either own land concessions in Indonesia or have related companies that do.
 The notices followed earlier ones, issued under Section 9 of the THPA to 10 Indonesian companies on 16 and 19 Oct, asking how they were preventing or suppressing fires on their lands. Firms face no penalties for not responding to notices under that section.
